name: Ngomba
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: No phonology of Ngomba (jgo) located online; Wikipedia stub cites only Ethnologue; SIL search blocked (403)

new_statements.quote: Tone is an indispensible part of the sound system of Ngomba and is just as important as the segmentals. There are many lexical items which are distinguished only by tone, e.g., [káŋ] 'plate' and [kàŋ] 'squirrel'. Tone is essential not only because it carries a high lexical load, but also because of its grammatical functions. [...] 6.1 Tone Inventory. Ngomba has two basic tones: 1. H (HIGH) 2. L (LOW). Phonetically one also finds a M (MID) tone, but I believe this to be a downstepped High. [...] Phonetically one finds the contours: F, a high-low falling tone, R a low-high rising tone and RF a rise-fall. One may view these as sequences of basic tones, as is common in African languages.
new_statements.citation: Satre, Scott A. 1997. Phonological Sketch of Ngomba. Yaoundé: SIL Cameroon / Ministère de la Recherche Scientifique et Technique. 32 pp. (ms. dated 19 Nov 1997; SIL Language & Culture Archives 47833)
new_statements.locator: §6 Tone, p. 26, and §6.1 Tone Inventory, p. 27 (PDF pp. 27-28)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (36-page scan, no text layer) and rendered PDF pp. 27-28, which carry printed page numbers 26 and 27. The page images show "6. TONE" at the foot of p. 26 with, verbatim, "Tone is an indispensible part of the sound system of Ngomba and is just as important as the segmentals. There are many lexical items which are distinguished only by tone, e.g., [káŋ] 'plate' and [kàŋ] 'squirrel'. Tone is essential not only because it carries a high lexical load, but also because of its grammatical functions." and on p. 27 "6.1 Tone Inventory / Ngomba has two basic tones : 1. H (HIGH) 2. L (LOW) / Phonetically one also finds a M (MID) tone, but I believe this to be a downstepped High." and "Phonetica…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given: the description treats Ngomba as a two-tone language (H, L, with downstep and phonetic contours) and never mentions stress, accent or prominence. The section headed 'Prosodies' (§4.2) concerns palatalization, labialization and length, not stress. The same holds for Ngouagna 1988 (p. 17: 'Le parler njinda est une langue à tons' — the Njinda variety is a tone language; six phonetic tone levels, four tonemes) and for Satre 2010 (SAL 39(1): 36, two basic tones L and H).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: None; no stress statement exists to have exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone (lexical roots mostly monosyllabic, CV(C) with 'echo vowel' in long closed syllables) plus grammatical/concord tone at phrase level; Satre also distinguishes phrase-final falling L from level L°. Nothing on stress at word or phrase level.
new_statements.identity_note: Both phonologies describe the Bamendjinda (Njinda) village variety, the SIL reference dialect of Ngomba (ALCAM 940); the other varieties are Bamesso, Bamenkoumbo, Babete and Bamendjo. Ngouagna 1988 names his object 'le parler njinda' and treats it as part of 'l'aire ngomba'. No separate glottocode for the Bamendjinda variety; it falls under ngom1272. Not to be confused with Ngombale [nla] (ngom1271), a different Bamileke language.
